text: It's tempting to picture attackers constantly hunting brand-new, never-seen vulnerabilities. In practice, most real-world breaches don't need one at all. A huge share of successful intrusions exploit known, already-patched flaws — bugs the vendor fixed months or even years earlier, on machines that simply never installed the update. Every unpatched system is attack surface that's effectively been handed to the attacker in writing, which is exactly why patch management is one of the highest-leverage jobs an administrator does.

Every patch moves through the same basic lifecycle. A vulnerability is discovered and disclosed, often with a public CVE identifier attached to it. The vendor releases a fix — for Microsoft, usually timed to Patch Tuesday. Rather than pushing that fix to every machine immediately, an administrator first deploys it to a small pilot ring of test machines and watches for crashes or driver conflicts over a few days. Only once nothing breaks does the same update roll out to the rest of the fleet.

Patch Tuesday is Microsoft's long-standing practice of releasing most security updates on the second Tuesday of every month. Microsoft settled on that cadence so IT departments could plan around a known, predictable release date instead of being surprised at random times — easy to put on a calendar and build a testing process around. When a vulnerability is severe enough, such as one already being actively exploited in the wild, Microsoft breaks that schedule with an out-of-band patch, shipped immediately instead of waiting for the next cycle.

That monthly cadence creates a real tension. Patch fast, and you close the exposure window before attackers can study the fix — security people call that risk Exploit Wednesday, since comparing patched and unpatched files can reveal the exact vulnerability within days. Patch carelessly, and an untested update can break a production application, driver, or configuration. Real organizations resolve this with a staged rollout: a pilot ring first, then the broader fleet on a set schedule, often within one to two weeks of the original release.

Patch Tuesday is only half the picture — it tells you when Microsoft ships updates, not how an organization with thousands of machines actually gets them installed. Next, the two real ways Windows environments manage that monthly flood of updates at scale: WSUS, a central server your machines check instead of the internet, and Windows Update for Business, managed entirely through cloud policy.
